clue.text: Passionate tale about leader of Mohicans

indicators.note: the leader of a group stands at its front, so only the opening letter of the next word is wanted
about means surrounding, so the word for a tale wraps around the other piece

explanation.surface: A stirring romantic yarn about the chief of the Mohicans, in the manner of Fenimore Cooper.
explanation.definitionFit: A stormy relationship or temperament is one full of violent, intense feeling, so the adjective is a synonym for passionate.

clue.text: Supernatural being priest exorcised

indicators.note: exorcising drives out and disrupts, so the letters of the cleric are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A ghostly presence driven out of a house by a clergyman.
explanation.definitionFit: A sprite is a fairy or elf, a small spirit from folklore, which is a kind of supernatural creature.

clue.text: Come up with chest missing lid

indicators.note: the lid is the top of a down entry, so the word loses its first letter

blocks.note: a coffer is a strongbox or chest

explanation.surface: Finding a treasure chest that has lost its lid.
explanation.definitionFit: To come up with something, such as a suggestion or a sum, is to put it forward, which is to offer it.

clue.text: Mother ringing rep bringing colour

indicators.note: to ring something is to encircle it, so the word for mother goes around the other

blocks.note: Ma is an informal word for mother
a sales rep acts as an agent

explanation.surface: Mum phones a sales representative who arrives bringing some cheer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ringing' suggests a phone call, but it means placing one word around another.
explanation.definitionFit: Magenta is a purplish-red hue, so it is an example of a colour.

clue.text: Sheepdog the lads let loose around noon

indicators.note: letting something loose sets it free to wander, so the letters scatter into a new order
around says the rearranged letters surround the short abbreviation

explanation.surface: Lads letting their sheepdog run free at midday.
explanation.definitionFit: The Shetland sheepdog, or sheltie, is a breed from the Scottish islands, so the name is a type of sheepdog.

clue.text: Brash types cheer Plantagenet king and son

blocks.note: Henry II, III, IV, V and VI were Plantagenet kings
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: Loud people applauding a medieval monarch and his heir.
explanation.walkthrough: A Hooray Henry is British slang for a loud, braying upper-class young man.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes boisterous, ostentatious young toffs, which matches brash people well.

clue.text: At that point, theatre collapsed

indicators.note: a building that has collapsed is in ruins, so its letters fall into a different arrangement

explanation.surface: A report that the playhouse fell down at that very moment.
explanation.definitionFit: Thereat is an old-fashioned adverb meaning there or at that time, so it fits a phrase about a particular point.

clue.text: To mollify everyone, I've turned up and dined

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning something upward means reading it from the bottom, so it runs backwards

explanation.surface: Someone arriving to dine in order to keep the whole party happy.
explanation.definitionFit: To alleviate is to ease or lessen distress, which is close to soothing or pacifying, the sense of mollify.

clue.text: Move to a smaller property in depressed area

blocks.note: an area is a measure of size

explanation.surface: Moving to a smaller home in a run-down neighbourhood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Depressed area' looks like a single poor district, but it splits into two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To downsize is to reduce scale, and in housing it means selling up for a smaller home.

clue.text: Good for son inside to decline asylum

indicators.note: one thing for another means swapping it in its place, and inside says the swap happens within the word

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good
S is the abbreviation for son, the letter removed
to decline an offer is to refuse it

explanation.surface: A good son reluctantly turning down the offer of sanctuary.
explanation.walkthrough: The S in the middle of the verb is replaced by G.
explanation.definitionFit: Asylum is protection or shelter given to someone in danger, which is what a refuge offers.

clue.text: Salad we locals ordered

indicators.note: ordered here means put into order, so the letters are arranged afresh

explanation.surface: Regulars at the pub telling you what they asked for with their meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ordered' looks like requesting food, which suits the salad, but it signals rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: Coleslaw is a dish of shredded raw cabbage in dressing, a kind of salad.

clue.text: Play a sly trick to attract individual after a hunger strike?

indicators.note: after places the word for individual behind the phrase for a hunger strike

blocks.note: a hunger strike is a fast, a refusal to eat

explanation.surface: Seeking sympathy and attention by refusing food.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that a hunger strike is only a fast in a loose sense.
explanation.definitionFit: To pull a fast one is an idiom for deceiving someone with a crafty trick.

clue.text: Spider coming from altar - aunt going berserk

indicators.note: going berserk means running wild, so the letters are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: A spider crawls out from behind the church altar and an aunt panics.
explanation.definitionFit: The tarantula is a large hairy species of spider, so it is an example of one.

clue.text: Brownies in chapel vestry

indicators.note: in says the solution lies inside the run of words that follows

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: Junior Girl Guides meeting in the church vestry.
explanation.walkthrough: Brownies are the youngest Girl Guides, but here they are the helpful household goblins of folklore.
explanation.definitionFit: A brownie in folklore is a small helpful sprite, a member of the same family of little people.

clue.text: Everything connected with the subject mentioned in New Orleans?

blocks.note: surface reading: a catch-all phrase for related matters
setter's reading: the birthplace of jazz would name that music among the matters

explanation.walkthrough: The stock phrase for 'and everything else of that kind' ends with the name of the music New Orleans is famous for, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom tacks on all the related stuff without listing it, which is everything connected with the topic.

clue.text: Happy hour binge for one next door

indicators.note: happy here suggests tipsy and merry, so the letters reel into a new order

explanation.surface: A happy-hour drinking session for the person who lives next door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Happy hour' reads as one bar term, but the first word works alone on the following two.
explanation.definitionFit: A neighbour is a person living in the adjacent house, the one next door.

clue.text: Is serial broadcast for Middle-Easterners?

indicators.note: broadcast also means scattered widely, like seed, so the letters are strewn into a new order

explanation.surface: Asking whether a TV drama series is being aired for a Middle Eastern audience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' looks like television, which suits 'serial', but it means scattered.
explanation.definitionFit: Israelis are citizens of Israel, a country in the Middle East.

clue.text: Prone to pilfering, as Bunter often was

blocks.note: second meaning: literally having fingers smeared with food

explanation.walkthrough: Billy Bunter is the greedy, cake-guzzling schoolboy of the Greyfriars stories, so his hands were often messy with jam and toffee.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone with light, grasping hands that things stick to is a habitual petty thief, a light-fingered type.

clue.text: Shelters for animals, well-groomed, reared round outskirts of Nuneaton

indicators.note: to rear up is to rise, and in a down clue going upward reads a word backwards
the outskirts of a town are its edges, so only the first and last letters count
round says the backwards word is placed around the edge letters

blocks.note: the outer letters of Nuneaton, a town in Warwickshire

explanation.surface: Animal shelters on the edge of a Midlands town raising smart-looking dogs.
explanation.definitionFit: Kennels are houses or establishments where dogs are kept, so they are shelters for animals.

clue.text: Inspect former pit, going after answer

indicators.note: going after places the word for a pit behind the abbreviation

blocks.note: A is the abbreviation for answer
a pit is a coal mine

explanation.surface: Checking a disused coal pit once the answer has been found.
explanation.definitionFit: To examine something is to look at it closely, a synonym for inspect.

clue.text: Man from ancient city calling for immediate attention?

blocks.note: Ur was a city of ancient Mesopotamia, a crossword favourite

explanation.surface: A man from an ancient city shouting for help.
explanation.definitionFit: Something urgent is pressing and demands to be dealt with straight away.

clue.text: A female, initially nervous, is pale-faced

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of the word before is used

explanation.surface: A nervous woman has gone white in the face.
explanation.definitionFit: Ashen means grey or white like ash, which describes a pale face drained of colour.

clue.text: Messy part upset M, say

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and disordered, so the letters fall out of order

explanation.surface: A boss annoyed about an untidy bit of work.
explanation.walkthrough: M is the head of the secret service in the James Bond stories; 'say' marks him as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: M runs the spies of MI6 in Ian Fleming's novels, making him an example of a spy chief.

clue.text: Feel spot

blocks.note: first meaning: to handle with the fingers
second meaning: a small amount, as in a spot of milk

explanation.definitionFit: The word is both the verb for making contact by hand and a noun for a trace or small quantity.

clue.text: Watched king brought in by Cornish town lecturer

indicators.note: being brought in by something means being taken inside it

blocks.note: Looe is a fishing town in Cornwall
K is the chess abbreviation for king
a don is a university lecturer

explanation.surface: A monarch escorted into a Cornish town by an academic while onlookers watch.
explanation.walkthrough: Looe is a small seaside town in Cornwall, in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: To look on is to be a spectator without taking part, so looked on means watched.

clue.text: Very small amount of time

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as one phrase about a brief moment, but splits into an adjective and a noun spelt alike and said differently.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means tiny and the noun is the unit of sixty seconds.

clue.text: Emphasised sweet dishes must be returned

indicators.note: something returned is sent back, so the word is read back to front

explanation.surface: A diner insisting the puddings be sent back to the kitchen.
explanation.definitionFit: A stressed word or syllable is one given extra weight or emphasis in speech.

clue.text: Very busy with calls, daughter in other resort

indicators.note: in places the abbreviation inside the following word
to re-sort is to sort again, so the letters are put into a fresh order

blocks.note: D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A holiday resort switchboard swamped with calls, a daughter stuck in another one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resort' looks like a holiday spot, but read as re-sort it means rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: Phone lines described as red-hot are ringing constantly, which is being extremely busy with calls.
